messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Niran is a 24-year-old painter who came to treatment months after the end of an abusive relationship with a male partner who had become increasingly controlling and violent in the small apartment they once shared. He described one night in particular when an argument turned physical near the front door. His partner had blocked the exit, watched him closely for any sign he might leave, and kept him pinned in the apartment long enough that the space itself began to feel like a trap. What stayed with Niran was not a clean story from beginning to end but flashes: the look of someone staring him down, the sense of waiting for the next move, the terrible uncertainty while seconds stretched and he did not know what would happen next. Those details help explain why, now, the feeling of being watched, moments of uncertainty, and sudden unwanted thoughts about the abuse strike him so forcefully in ordinary life.

In the weeks afterward, he tried hard to manage what broke through. As evening came, he would keep himself busy with errands, videos, or scrolling on his phone because bedtime felt dangerous; he had learned that quiet, dark stretches of the day were when dreams came closest. He also went out of his way to avoid anything that reminded him of his former partner, taking different streets to his studio and refusing invitations to neighborhoods they used to visit together. When something startled him or felt even vaguely confrontational, he found himself going completely still, the same way he had during the abuse. These habits made sense to him as protection, especially when an unwanted thought or the sense that someone was observing him suddenly flared.

The same triggers also kept his body on alert. At work, if a client was late unlocking a building or a supervisor took too long to answer a text, Niran immediately assumed something bad was happening. Entering galleries, apartment lobbies, or supply stores, he scanned for exits before he could focus on paint colors or the wall in front of him. At home he listened for sounds near the door, straining to catch any sign that someone might be coming in. The feeling of uncertainty was especially potent; any delay seemed loaded with threat, and the sense of being watched made enclosed places feel unsafe.

His memories remained disjointed and vivid in a way he found hard to explain. Some moments of the abuse were painfully clear—the stance by the door, the stare, the suspended instant before he knew what would happen—while other stretches were blank. He could not put the sequence in order, and when an image did come, he did not experience it as a past event but as if it were happening again right now. The unwanted thoughts did not stay abstract for long; they tipped into reliving, and that reliving made him even more certain he had to stay on guard.

Over time, the way he understood the abuse darkened. Because he had frozen and because he had stayed in the relationship as long as he did, Niran had come to believe the violence said something essential about him: that it happened because of the kind of person he was, that he was inadequate, that he no longer really belonged anywhere. Those beliefs sharpened his sensitivity to other people’s attention. If someone glanced at him too long on the train or in a worksite hallway, he felt exposed at once, as though others could see the weakness he despised in himself. Once that feeling took hold, he watched doors, listened for entry sounds, and braced for harm more intensely.

The cycle tightened through his efforts to cope. Avoiding reminders of his ex narrowed his world and left the memories less tested by ordinary life; they returned in abrupt, fragmented bursts that felt current rather than finished. Staying up to avoid dreams meant he was exhausted, and in that tired state he was more easily flooded by unwanted thoughts at work. Freezing whenever he felt threatened left him ashamed afterward, which fed his sense of inadequacy and made future moments of uncertainty even more charged. The more he scanned for exits and listened for danger, the more often he noticed signs that seemed to confirm he was not safe, and those cues pulled up the same broken pieces of memory again.

By the time he sought help, the effects had become visible in his daily life. He was missing deadlines on painting jobs because he lost time checking entrances and waiting for his body to settle, and his partner now found him distant and unreachable at night, when he would resist going to bed and tense at every noise in the apartment. Niran came in frightened by how quickly a delay, a look, or an unwanted thought could make the past feel present. More than anything, he feared that this constant vigilance meant he had been permanently changed into someone weak and out of place; at the same time, he still hoped treatment might help him sleep, work, and feel that his life belongs to him again.
